# Budget game screen workbook

Revised copy and implementation plan for the new age bands

Use the revised copy beside each historical screenshot, then follow the age progression and build plan at the end. Screen IDs stay stable. Screenshots show the earlier prototype; editable copy and the revised specifications define the next build.

Source: https\://budget-game-curiotell.vercel.app/  
Captured 15 November 2026  \|  Mobile viewport 390 × 844

# **Sections**

[Getting started    5 captures](#bookmark=id.thugi3x4a4a2)

[Ages 6 to 8    36 captures](#bookmark=id.vzh2vfcr5wf0)

[Ages 8 to 11    34 captures](#bookmark=id.w1nap4gevzq5)

[Ages 11 to 15    50 captures](#bookmark=id.c1e3qv16pewj)

[Observed issues    1 captures](#bookmark=id.8jf9qjvqkben)

## **How to use the references**

G \= shared screens, A \= ages 6–8, B \= ages 8–11, C \= ages 11–15, Z \= observed issue. The IDs still name the original screenshot files. New screen specifications are included in the revised build plan.

Captures show complete playthroughs, examples, menus, story replays and selected feedback branches. Amounts and answer order can vary between runs. Repeated layouts with different numerical combinations are represented by the captured examples.

# **Age progression and revised build plan**

The revised games develop different decisions across ages 6–8, 8–11 and 11–15. The youngest player builds an affordable game day. The middle player buys enough for a group and protects the event when attendance changes. The oldest player matches supplies to the stall’s requirements and manages payment dates. Clarity and understanding take priority over the number of taps. Every explanation should use complete, friendly sentences, with visuals showing the same thing.

The screenshots show the previous prototype. The copy beside each screenshot and the specifications below describe the revised build. Keep the reference IDs and screenshot archive for implementation; do not treat prices, age labels or old questions baked into those images as current requirements. New screens are written out below. The document specifies the changes; the app still needs to implement them.

“Looks good” identifies an existing layout or interaction worth retaining. It does not approve an unclear explanation. Give a first-time player the context, rules and visual demonstration needed to make the next choice. Additional help and replays remain available. A familiar returning player may skip an explanation, but do not leave essential context hidden behind an optional hint.

## **The progression at a glance**

| Age band | Core decision | New challenge | Evidence of success |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 6–8 | Can I afford my game day? | One activity; optional stickers; snack-price rise. | Needs plus one activity within ₹100. |
| 8–11 | Can the budget serve everyone? | Pack quantities; two stations; 20 children become 24\. | Enough servings and two stations within ₹600. |
| 11–15 | Can I pay on the due dates? | Kit capacity; sponsor timing; payment schedules. | At least 40 sets and no uncovered due-day bill. |

## **School references and the quality standard**

NCERT’s stage structure places ages 8–11 broadly in Grades 3–5, while ages 11–15 cross the middle and early secondary stages. Use age as a starting guide and let a player request support or an extension. This is selected skill and teaching-approach mapping, rather than a complete syllabus map. \[1\]

NCERT/PARAKH’s foundational expectations include fluent two-digit addition and subtraction and simple money transactions up to ₹100. This supports beginning A with a ₹100 budget, visual money and optional read-aloud. Published elementary learning outcomes include simple bills and practical number operations, supporting B’s quantities, pack comparisons and group planning. \[2\]\[3\]

Cambridge Primary and Lower Secondary Mathematics emphasise applying computation to everyday situations and supporting a solution with evidence. IB PYP emphasises meaningful inquiry, learner choice and reflection. IB MYP Mathematics emphasises representing real situations, applying strategies and evaluating solutions. These are useful quality references for the decisions and feedback, while child-facing language stays plain. \[4\]\[5\]\[6\]\[7\]

| Reference | Relevant skill or approach | How the game uses it |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| NCERT / CBSE | Money operations; quantities; simple bills. | A visual affordability; B snack purchases and group planning. |
| Cambridge Primary / Lower Secondary | Reasoning, applying methods and evidence. | Compare packs or payment plans; test a change and inspect the result. |
| IB PYP | Inquiry, learner choice and reflection. | Choose an affordable event and explain a specific decision. |
| IB MYP Mathematics | Model real situations; apply and evaluate a solution. | C ledger, delayed income and comparison of viable schedules. |

Build the quality into the task through a clear situation, meaningful choices and feedback that explains the result. Use as many taps as the explanation needs, with a clear next action on each one. Split a difficult idea into understandable steps instead of trimming away meaning. Keep adult curriculum names out of the game, and let the words, pictures and changing amounts explain the same event. Smooth pacing means the child understands what happens next, not that the game has fewer screens.

## **Age routing and difficulty**

Display the agreed labels 6–8, 8–11 and 11–15. For exact-age routing, use 6 ≤ age \< 8, 8 ≤ age \< 11 and 11 ≤ age ≤ 15\. At 8 and 11, default to the next band. Let families manually select another band. This resolves overlap without changing the agreed labels.

Within 6–8, offer read-aloud, pictures and counting support. Within 8–11, demonstrate one serving per child and how pack quantities affect the order before asking for a purchase. Within 11–15, introduce the stall and the difference between current and future money, then guide a live payment row. Extra taps are welcome whenever they clarify an unfamiliar idea. Returning players can reopen explanations or move past familiar ones. The tougher event remains an extension within the same age band.

## **A ages 6 to 8**

Learning goal: choose one activity while keeping required items and the total within the money available. Core budget ₹100. Required supplies ₹20 and snacks ₹20 are added automatically and visibly cost money. Activities: Puzzles ₹30, Crafts ₹40, Team games ₹50. Pick exactly one. Stickers are optional at ₹20.

The twist changes snacks from ₹20 to ₹40. Only this price changes. Pause with Mira’s message, then show the old snack price becoming the new price and the total rising by ₹20. Keep supplies and snacks under NEEDS, the required activity under ACTIVITIES, and stickers under OPTIONAL EXTRAS. The player may remove stickers or swap the activity. A final total of ₹100 is valid. Give a visual example and more explanation taps whenever needed.

First-play flow: A01–A02 establish game day → A04 explains the task → A09 reveals NEEDS, the activity choice and optional stickers → A14 reviews the first plan → A19 pauses for the price-change message and visual reveal → A20 checks understanding → A24 opens editable choices if needed → A26 reviews the result → A32 shows the actual game day → A33 connects the result to the decision. A03, A05–A08, A15–A18 and A27–A31 provide definitions, demonstrations and reflection as needed. Do not shorten the first explanation just to reduce taps.

Worked acceptance case: Crafts plus stickers initially costs ₹20 \+ ₹20 \+ ₹40 \+ ₹20 \= ₹100. After the snack rise the same selection costs ₹120. Removing stickers returns it to exactly ₹100. A second valid approach is to choose Puzzles without stickers, which ends at ₹90. An original Puzzles-only plan already survives, changing from ₹70 to ₹90, and should not require a repair.

Keep the author’s early headings and first-person story. Retain the request to place money available at the top right of example cards in bold green, and to emphasise the result. Keep Back visually secondary and Skip inside the story box; preserve an easy tap area. Read-aloud must match the visible wording.

## **B ages 8 to 11**

Learning goal: make a budget serve a stated group. Core brief: 20 children, two different activity stations, one snack serving per child and a ₹600 budget. Show three distinct groups: NECESSITIES includes the required room and snacks; ACTIVITIES says Choose TWO and is also required; ADD-ONS contains optional decorations. Room ₹100 is already included. Every activity option supports up to 30 children, and all children rotate through both stations. Do not imply that activities are optional because they sit outside NECESSITIES.

Snack packs: 10 servings cost ₹100; 20 servings cost ₹180. The player can buy multiple packs or mix the pack sizes. A serving means one child’s snack. Show pack count, total servings, children covered and snack cost together. For 20 children, one large pack costs ₹180 and two small packs cost ₹200. Either is a valid affordable choice; a comparison question asks explicitly when the goal is lowest cost.

Activity prices: Puzzles ₹120; Team games ₹100; Crafts with new materials ₹120 or reused materials ₹80. Crafts count as one station whichever material option is used. Both material choices provide the same capacity and activity. New materials look fresh; reused materials have mixed colours. Optional decorations cost ₹40. No preparation timer or hidden quality penalty is added.

The twist changes attendance from 20 to 24 children. Prices and activity capacity stay unchanged. Bought snack packs remain in the plan and cannot be returned; explain this before the original order is placed. After the twist, extra snack packs are a DRAFT until the whole revised plan is checked and confirmed. The player may edit these pending packs as well as activity choices, craft materials and decorations. Only the original bought packs stay locked. This makes every new choice reviewable and avoids ordering unaffordable extras before seeing the whole effect.

First-play flow: B01 introduces Mira and Quest Day → B02 and NEW B02a show the things we need and what is optional → B04 explains what the player will choose → NEW B08a demonstrates servings and lets the player plan the snack order → B09 chooses activities and optional decorations → B14 reviews the whole plan before placing the snack order → B19 pauses for the four new children → B20–B23 explain and check snack coverage → NEW B23a adds draft extra packs if needed → B24 reviews the whole plan and its editable choices → B29 confirms a valid final plan → B30 shows the event → B31 connects choices to outcomes. Definitions, examples and reflection can take more taps whenever they help. The number of screens is not a success measure.

Keep the room and snacks visibly labelled REQUIRED, show the two activity spaces as required choices, and label decorations OPTIONAL. Beside each section, show what is included, what is still missing and where the child can make a choice. Keep Your budget ₹600, Your plan ₹{total} and Money left ₹{remaining} together, or show ₹{over} over your budget. When one check fails, explain that check beside the relevant choice. Show exact quantities as well as colours or ticks.

## **NEW B08a buying the snacks**

Insert after B04 and before B09.

Heading: Snacks for Everyone

Body: 20 children are coming to Quest Day. Let’s get a snack for everyone\! You need to buy at least 20 servings. Each serving is for one child only.

Pack cards: This pack has 10 servings and costs ₹100. / This pack has 20 servings and costs ₹180.

Summary: You have chosen {servings} servings for 20 children. These snacks cost ₹{snackCost}.

Button: Use these packs in my plan.

Visual: Keep NECESSITIES visible, with Room ₹100 already included and Snacks marked Required, choose the packs. Open one example pack and give one serving to each child before enabling the independent choice.

Supporting line: These packs are in our plan. We will order them when you confirm the whole plan.

Before final confirmation at B14: Once we place the snack order, we cannot return those packs. We can still change the activities and decorations.

If short: {missingServings} children still need a snack each. Let’s add a pack so everyone gets one.

Show Add a pack and Remove a pack controls with pack count, servings and price. A highlighted card alone does not explain whether a pack is selected, added to the plan or already bought; label those states explicitly.

## **NEW B23a adding snacks for the larger group**

Reuse the snack-pack layout after B23 when coverage is short.

Heading: 4 more children decided to join. Do we need more snacks?

Body: We now need snacks for 24 children. You’ve already bought {boughtServings} servings. Let’s add a few more so the new children get a snack too.

Bought section: These packs are already bought. They stay in our plan.

Choice section: Choose extra packs to add to our plan.

Summary: With these extra packs, we would have {servings} servings for 24 children. The snacks would cost ₹{snackCost} altogether.

Buttons: Add these packs to our plan. / Go back to my choices.

Show the original packs separately from draft extra packs. The four new child places appear in the same group, and each serving fills one place. Once 24 are filled, label any remaining servings Extra servings rather than inventing extra children. Show the full event total before moving on. Draft extras remain editable until the whole revised plan is valid and confirmed at B29. If the initial order already covers 24, show “We already have enough snacks for everyone. We don’t need to buy more,” then return to the whole plan.

## **B valid solutions and useful feedback**

Canonical initial plan: Room ₹100 \+ one large snack pack ₹180 \+ Puzzles ₹120 \+ new Crafts ₹120 \+ Decorations ₹40 \= ₹560, leaving ₹40. It has 20 servings and both stations support 30 children. Four new children require at least one extra small pack at ₹100. The unchanged event then costs ₹660, which is ₹60 over.

Solution preserving the original stations: change new Crafts to reused materials, saving ₹40, and remove decorations, saving ₹40. Final cost ₹580, with 30 servings and ₹20 left. Another valid solution preserves decorations: reused Crafts ₹80 \+ Team games ₹100 \+ room ₹100 \+ 30 snack servings ₹280 \+ decorations ₹40 \= ₹600. New Crafts plus Team games without decorations is also ₹600. Reward the decision the player made.

A child who initially bought two small packs has already spent ₹200 for 20 servings. Adding a third small pack brings snack spending to ₹300. Room ₹100 \+ reused Crafts ₹80 \+ Team games ₹100 \+ snacks ₹300 \= ₹580. Do not replace the old order with a cheaper hypothetical large pack after the purchase has been confirmed. Every valid initial purchase must retain at least one feasible repair.

Example feedback by problem: “Four children still need a snack each.” “You have enough snacks. But your plan is ₹60 over your budget.” “Removing decorations saves ₹40. We still need to cut ₹20 more.” “You kept decorations by choosing reused crafts and team games.” These follow the author’s fuller, friendly style. Use the actual child count, saving, remaining shortfall and chosen activities. Point each message to the corresponding visual or choice; never show a generic rejection in its place.

## **C ages 11 to 15**

Learning goal: prepare enough supplies and pay every bill using money available when it is due. Make the stall concrete: card-and-bookmark sets for a school pop-up. Core brief requires at least 40 sets. This is a preparation and payment mission. Capacity is not revenue, and money left is not profit.

Kit capacities and prices: Small makes 20 sets and costs ₹900; Medium makes 40 sets and costs ₹1,800; Big makes 60 sets and costs ₹2,300 when paid Wednesday or ₹2,400 when paid Friday. Medium can be paid ₹1,800 Wednesday or split into ₹1,000 Wednesday and ₹800 next Monday. Small belongs to a clearly labelled 20-set replay and fails the core 40-set requirement. Extra capacity does not automatically earn a bonus.

Core schedule: ₹2,500 starting money Monday; ₹700 sponsor payment expected Friday; optional posters ₹250 Friday; required cleanup ₹200 Saturday. The twist moves only the sponsor payment to next Monday. The total promised amount stays the same. At each checkpoint the game first adds that day’s income, then deducts bills due that day. State this model and use an undated week strip.

First-play flow: C01 and NEW C01a introduce Mira, the stall and one finished set → C02 and NEW C02a distinguish the money available now from the sponsor’s later payment → C03 and NEW C03a separate necessities from optional posters → C04 explains the player’s task → C05 explains why a changed date might matter → C06 shows the route through planning → NEW C10a defines the kit quantities → C11–C13 make the kit and payment choice → C14–C15 choose extras → C16 guides the live payment days → C17 reviews the first result → C23–C25 clearly introduce the sponsor’s delay → C26 checks the first uncovered day → C30–C38 explain and test changes → C44 shows the finished stall → C45 connects the result to the choices. Worked examples, comparisons and reasoning remain available. Add explanatory taps where needed, especially on first play.

## **NEW C01a a concrete stall and role**

Heading: Here’s what we’re making for the stall.

Mira: Each set has one card and one bookmark, packed together. We need at least 40 complete sets for our school pop-up. I’ll take care of the display. Will you help me choose the supplies and work out when we can pay for everything?

Button: Show me the money we have.

Visual: Show a real finished card-and-bookmark set first. Then build a labelled group of 40 sets, using countable groups. Point to the empty supply space and the display so the player can see what they are helping plan.

Keep the 40-set requirement visible beside kit selection and the final ledger. No sales target or selling price is added. The sponsor funds the activity; it is not a customer payment in disguise.

## **NEW C10a understanding the kits**

Heading: What do we get in a supplies kit?

Body: A kit gives us card blanks, bookmark materials and packing supplies. Each card and bookmark are packed together to make one complete set. We need supplies for at least 40 complete sets, so let’s compare how many each kit can make.

Cards: The small kit makes 20 sets. / The medium kit makes 40 sets. / The big kit makes 60 sets.

Button: Compare the kit prices and payment options.

Visual: Open the kit to show its materials, then show how they become finished sets. Pens and display tools are shared. Do not use an unexplained gift-box icon as the only description.

Define one set visually as one card and one bookmark, packaged together. Do not label 20 loose pieces as 20 finished sets. At C34, a Small selection gives the explicit 20-set shortage. The player cannot satisfy a 40-set brief simply by choosing the cheapest option.

## **Guided action inside C16**

Use the player’s live plan and explain one payment day in clear steps. First show “This is the money we have left from the previous day.” Next reveal any money arriving today. Then introduce the named bill and amount due today. Let the player tap to see whether that money covers the payment and what is left. Carry that same amount visibly into the next day. Use as many taps as the explanation needs; keep the finished row readable and replayable.

Optional hint: That money is not available yet.

Supporting sentence: The sponsor’s ₹700 arrives on {sponsorDay}. We cannot use it before that day.

Point to the future sponsor card while giving this hint. Do not show it when the income has already arrived.

Keep the rule ₹0 or more. A negative forecast means we cannot pay that bill on time; it does not mean the game has lent us money. Child-facing labels are Money we have on Monday, Money left at the end, and Least money left after a payment day. Explain the last label on tap: “This is the smallest amount we would have left after paying the bills for any of the days shown.” Keep the first unpaid day distinct from the day with the largest shortage.

## **NEW C38a compare two payment plans**

Offer after a valid core Medium-kit solution with posters, using the same kit, extras and late sponsor date.

Heading: Which payment choice leaves us more money before Monday?

Body: Both choices pay for the same medium kit and cost ₹1,800 altogether. One pays it all on Wednesday. The other pays ₹1,000 on Wednesday and ₹800 next Monday. Let’s compare how much money is left on the days before the sponsor pays.

Buttons: Walk me through the first choice. / Walk me through the second choice.

Visual: Keep both labelled payment plans available and reveal comparable day rows. A tap switches which plan is explained without changing the player’s saved plan.

For the all-Wednesday choice, show ₹700 left Wednesday, ₹450 Friday, ₹250 Saturday and ₹950 next Monday. For the split choice, show ₹1,500 Wednesday, ₹1,250 Friday, ₹1,050 Saturday and ₹950 next Monday. Explanation: “Paying in two parts leaves us more money to use before Monday. Both plans still finish with ₹950 after all the payments.” Both are valid here. If these are not the player’s choices, label the comparison as an example. Never present another plan’s numbers as the child’s own result.

## **An optional tougher brief within ages 11 to 15**

After the core, offer “Try a tougher brief”. Starting money is ₹2,000. The stall still needs 40 sets. Posters ₹250 Friday and cleanup ₹200 Saturday are both required. Sponsor ₹700 is initially due Friday and later moves to next Monday. All these conditions appear before selection. The Medium kit retains the same payment choices. There is no hidden exemption or forced extra discovered at the end.

Medium upfront initially works: Wednesday ₹200; Friday ₹200 \+ ₹700 − ₹250 \= ₹650; Saturday ₹450; next Monday ₹450. After the delay it fails first on Friday by ₹50, with Saturday forecast −₹250, even though the final forecast returns to ₹450. Split payment solves it: Wednesday ₹1,000; Friday ₹750; Saturday ₹550; next Monday ₹550 \+ ₹700 − ₹800 \= ₹450.

The tougher brief makes timing consequential while keeping whole-rupee arithmetic. Require the 40 sets and both named bills; Small and removal of posters are not valid repairs. Different starting money is shown prominently so a returning child does not carry over the core ₹2,500. Percentages and profit calculations are future extensions, not extra entry requirements for the 11–15 core.

## **Worked checks for implementation**

| Scenario | Expected result | What it checks |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| A Crafts and stickers | ₹100 initially; ₹120 after the rise; ₹100 after removing stickers. | Exact-budget success and a valid repair. |
| B canonical plan | ₹560 initially; ₹660 after adding a small pack; ₹580 after materials and decorations changes. | Coverage and affordability are separate checks. |
| B preserve decorations | Room \+ 30 servings \+ reused Crafts \+ Team games \+ decorations \= ₹600. | More than one valid final plan. |
| C core Medium upfront | Late-sponsor balances: ₹700, ₹450, ₹250, ₹950 after Monday. | All bills covered; lowest day-end balance ₹250. |
| C core Medium split | Late-sponsor balances: ₹1,500, ₹1,250, ₹1,050, ₹950 after Monday. | Same final balance; more money available earlier. |
| C tougher upfront | ₹200 Wednesday; −₹50 Friday; −₹250 Saturday; ₹450 next Monday. | Positive ending does not erase the first shortfall. |
| C tougher split | ₹1,000 Wednesday; ₹750 Friday; ₹550 Saturday; ₹450 next Monday. | Split schedule covers every required bill. |

These are calculations for the proposed configuration, not results from a modified app. Enumeration checked all 27 valid initial Quest Day configurations under these prices: each has a feasible adjustment after the attendance change, and seven already cover 24 children. The app should repeat these checks against its actual state and validation logic.

## **Checks before the revised game is released**

All school and age references in headings, the picker and editable copy use the new bands. The older screenshots retain their original baked-in labels and amounts, which are explicitly historical. Keep screen IDs stable. Retitled B screens correspond to the new attendance twist, not the earlier snack-price change.

Update validation alongside text. A and C optional reason questions now have one correct answer. B’s prediction compares servings with the current guest count. B’s final validation checks snack coverage, exactly two different stations and total cost. C checks kit capacity and each due-day balance. Correct-answer positions may shuffle; store answer identity rather than the displayed letter.

B snack purchases use integer pack counts. Keep original bought packs locked, but treat extra packs after the attendance change as a draft until the whole revised event is checked and confirmed. Draft extra packs can be reduced or changed in B24. Compute servings, children missing a snack, costs and any shortfall from the same current plan. Every valid original purchase must allow a feasible final plan. All activity options retain capacity for 30 children.

Keep required costs separate from optional extras. Correct exactly-zero outcomes pass. Plans that already survive a twist can finish without a needless change. The current C37 blank ledger, C48 empty bills replay and Z01 blank story state still need fixes. Check whether the ₹351 badge is a transition capture or a rounding error; checked balances must be exact.

Help, story replay and comparison preserve the current plan. Story replay after a twist says “Starting brief”; it must not make the player think that the live guest count or sponsor date reset. Back returns to the current editable decision. The final event uses the selected activities, kit and optional extras.

Try the revised flow with children in each band. Check whether they can act without an adult explaining the missing context. Ask the younger player what must stay in the plan, the middle player whether everyone is covered and the older player which money is available before a bill. Use their actions and explanation to judge understanding. Record where help is needed and whether a second plan is chosen voluntarily.

# **Writing and visual flow guide**

The main design goal is that the child understands the situation, the choice and its consequence. There is no target number of taps. A new idea can take several screens or several guided steps on one screen. Keep those steps connected through the same character, objects and visible plan. Do not shorten a sentence until its meaning becomes an unexplained label.

## **How the game should speak to the child**

Use the author’s friendly, direct voice. Explain who is doing what, the amount or quantity involved, and what the child can do next. Say “You have enough snacks. But your plan is ₹60 over your budget,” rather than “Enough. Over ₹60.” Say “That money is not available yet,” while pointing to the future payment, rather than referring vaguely to a rule.

Write complete sentences for story, instruction and feedback. Short headings, button labels and stable group labels are still useful when their meaning is explained. Prefer “What will we need to pay for?” to “Bills”, and “Which is the first day we cannot pay all the bills?” to “Which bill comes too soon?” Do not add excitement words or exclamation marks in place of an explanation.

Keep Mira speaking in first person when she introduces her event, and use “we” for the plan the child helps make. Use “you” for the player’s choice. Explain “serving”, “set”, “supplies kit” and “sponsor” with the actual object or situation at their first use. Reserve “brief”, “capacity”, “ledger” and “cash flow” for adult notes unless the game explicitly teaches the term.

A feedback message should name what happened and connect it to something the child can inspect or change. It can take more than one tap to show the result, explain why and return to the editable choice. Keep the message available until the child is ready. Read-aloud repeats the same wording and does not remove the visible text.

## **NEW B02a separate necessities from optional extras**

Heading: Let’s see what our day needs.

Body: We need a room and snacks for everyone. We also need two different activities for the class to enjoy. Decorations can make the room look nice, but they are optional. We can leave them out if we need the money for something else.

Button: Let’s choose the snacks.

Visual: A labelled planning board reveals each section in turn. NECESSITIES has Room ₹100, already included, and Snacks, required, choose packs. ACTIVITIES has two empty spaces labelled Choose TWO. ADD-ONS has Decorations ₹40, optional.

Use complete labels and an explanation as each group is revealed. A lock icon alone does not say whether an item is needed, already bought or merely unavailable. Room says Required, already included. Snacks says Required, choose enough for everyone. Activities say Required, choose two. Decorations say Optional, you can leave these out. Preserve these groups in snack selection, plan review and repair, rather than showing the distinction only in the story.

## **Where choices are made in Quest Day**

The overview is a place to understand the task. The snack screen is where pack quantities change. Activity cards open their own choice panels; the Crafts panel contains the material choice. Decorations have an obvious add/remove control inside ADD-ONS. The child reviews the whole plan before the original snack order is placed. Never use the same tick, tap or animation to mean both “selected for the plan” and “already bought”.

On the snack screen, show a pack opening into servings, with one serving moving to each child. Make the child places and packs countable. Show the pack count, servings and price together as the plus or minus control is used. Keep the NECESSITIES section and the required room cost visible, even while the activity and extra sections are collapsed. Label the full-plan total; do not present it as money already spent before confirmation.

For a craft or decoration change, open one bottom sheet anchored to that item. Explain the choice with an object picture, price and what would change in the plan. Show the old total, the saving or added cost and the new total. Buttons say Keep this choice and Go back. The panel closes back to the same place, with the chosen item and its effect visible.

## **Introduce the attendance change before asking for a decision**

At B19, pause the planner and show Mira’s message that four more children have decided to join. On the next tap, four children join the existing group and the count changes from 20 to 24\. Keep the original packs in view. Do not silently recalculate a cost, instantly buy more snacks or jump directly to an error. The player first sees what changed, then counts the servings, then chooses whether more packs are needed.

NEW B23a keeps the already-bought packs in one labelled area and the extra packs being considered in another. After Add these packs to our plan, show how many children are covered and the full-plan total. Those extra packs are still editable until the revised whole plan is valid and confirmed. If changing another choice saves ₹40 but leaves ₹20 to cut, show both facts. This makes the child’s next action understandable.

## **NEW C02a explain money that arrives later**

Heading: When can we use the sponsor’s money?

Body: The sponsor has promised us ₹700 on Friday. That money is not available yet. We can use it only after it arrives. Until Friday, we need to use the ₹{startMoney} we already have.

Button: See what we need to pay for.

Visual: Monday’s money is in a labelled available-money area. The ₹700 stays on Friday with “Expected, not received yet”. Touching it before Friday opens the exact hint, “That money is not available yet,” and points to its arrival date.

This is a planning timeline, not a real-time countdown. Explain that we are working out what would happen on each payment day. In C16, money is added on the day it arrives before that day’s bills are paid. After the sponsor update, the same payment moves to next Monday. The child should not have to remember a definition to understand why it cannot cover an earlier bill.

## **NEW C03a show optional posters separately**

Heading: Some things are optional.

Body: We could add posters to decorate the stall. They cost ₹250 and need to be paid for on Friday. Posters are optional in this game, so it is okay to leave them out. You’ll decide whether to add them after choosing the supplies kit.

Button: Show me what I need to do.

Visual: Keep Supplies kit and Cleanup under NECESSITIES. Show Posters separately under ADD-ONS, clearly labelled Optional. This story card previews the choice; the actual poster selection happens at C14.

For the tougher event, use a separate full sentence: “This event needs posters too, so we must include ₹250 for them on Friday.” Show the corresponding required status from the start. Never let a child learn that a previously optional item has become mandatory only after making the plan.

## **Make the payment-day demonstration visible**

C16 starts with the player’s selected kit and extras. Focus one dated row, then show the money carried from the previous day, any income arriving now and the named bills due now. Let the child tap through those steps. After the subtraction, visibly carry the remaining amount to the next day. Keep a Replay this day action and the full timeline available. Pause after a surprising result so the child can inspect it.

A future income card stays in its future date while a bill is being considered earlier. If the child tries to count it, point to that card and say, “That money is not available yet.” Then name the relevant date. When a bill cannot be paid, show money available, bill amount and the amount missing together. Explain that a negative forecast is an unpaid bill, not permission to borrow. Exactly ₹0 after a payment still passes.

## **Use pop-ups when they explain an event or a choice**

Use an event message to introduce a changed fact, such as extra children or a delayed payment. Use a choice panel when the child opens an editable item, such as Crafts or a payment plan. Keep hints beside the thing they explain. Show only one overlay at a time, label its action and return to the same underlying screen. Keep important information visible after the panel closes, rather than making it exist only inside a temporary pop-up.

On mobile, keep the required/optional labels and current task visible while scrolling. Make selection states explicit in words. Buttons should say what happens next, such as Review our whole plan, rather than a vague Done when another decision follows. Do not auto-advance a story message before it has been read, and do not require precise timing to follow an animation. The child can replay a visual explanation.

## **Give the player a reason to try another plan**

Show the actual event the child created: chosen activities, craft materials, snacks and retained decorations in B; the chosen supplies and posters in C. Let a tap reveal how a choice affected the plan. A replay invitation names a new decision, such as keeping decorations with a different activity mix or comparing payment plans. Save the completed plan so the next valid plan can be compared with it.

Vary a stated requirement or event between authored replays, with each scenario checked for valid solutions. Keep those changes visible before choices are made. Recognition should explain what the player achieved, and the game should offer a clear stopping point. Whether children voluntarily return and can explain the concept must be checked in playtesting; extra taps or a particular phrase do not by themselves prove engagement.

## **Quest Day visual sequence**

| Moment | What the child sees | Where the choice happens | What explains the result |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Needs | Room and snacks under NECESSITIES; two required activity spaces; optional decorations. | The overview explains these groups before buying. | Each item says required, optional, already included or still to choose. |
| Snack order | A pack opens into servings; one serving goes to each child. | Pack plus/minus controls show price, quantity and servings together. | The covered group and remaining children update with the same action. |
| Activities | Two empty spaces fill with selected activity scenes. | An activity panel; Crafts contains its material choices. | Old total, price change and new total stay together. |
| First review | The whole event and its total; a snack-order confirmation. | Review choices or place the original snack order. | A receipt marks only those packs as bought. |
| Four join | Mira’s message; four new children; count moves 20 to 24\. | First count existing servings, then consider extra packs. | Original packs stay visible; any child without a serving is shown. |
| Revised plan | Bought packs and draft extras are separate; editable activities and decorations. | Add draft packs or change a draft item, then review. | Explain the saving, remaining shortfall and eventual valid event. |

## **Pop-up visual sequence**

| Moment | What the child sees | Where the choice happens | What explains the result |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Stall | One complete card-and-bookmark set, then the 40-set target. | Story introduces the product and player’s role. | The same target remains beside the kit cards. |
| Money | Monday’s usable money; Friday’s expected sponsor payment. | A guided date demonstration before independent planning. | The future payment has a date and Not available yet label. |
| Costs | Required kit and cleanup; posters separately optional. | The story previews costs; kit selection and C14 make choices. | Every chosen bill has its name, amount and due day. |
| Payment choice | Exact kit quantities and one or two dated payments. | A kit/payment panel shows the options before confirmation. | The selected dates and amounts update the same timeline. |
| Check days | One row reveals carried money, arrivals, bills and money left. | The child steps through a day or opens another day’s details. | Future income stays in the future; missing money is shown beside the bill. |
| Delay and repair | Sponsor message; ₹700 moves to next Monday; bills stay put. | Compare an editable choice beside the first uncovered bill. | Before/after dates and balances explain whether the change helped. |

## **What the external examples suggest**

PBS’s official description of Cyberchase Railway Hero discusses more than one combination of track lengths that can repair the same gap. The relevant application here is to let a child inspect different valid plans and see the result of each choice. Khan Academy Kids’ official math overview describes guided prompts, visual models and in-the-moment support. The relevant application is to explain the money or serving problem beside the action. These are design interpretations of published examples, not claims from a hands-on test of those apps.

Game-design references: PBS KIDS, Supporting Your Child With Disabilities With Digital Learning Games, including Railway Hero: https\://www\.pbs.org/parents/thrive/supporting-your-child-with-disabilities-with-digital-learning-games . Khan Academy Kids, Math Support App: https\://www\.khanacademy.org/kids/math . The youngest reference audience informs visual support; it does not set the tone for 11–15-year-olds.
